draft.title: Changes to the Murray-Darling Basin
card: Dams, weirs and taking water for irrigation have changed the Murray-Darling Basin. Rivers carry less water and flows are different from before.
Taking large amounts of water for use on farms and in towns leaves less water in the rivers. Wetlands can dry out, and low flows can leave fish and other water life short of habitat.
Dams and weirs change when and how much water flows downstream. Irrigation can raise saline water tables. Low flows then no longer flush salt out to sea, so salinity builds up.
Algal blooms can form when water is warm, slow and low and has extra nutrients, such as fertiliser washed off farms. Blooms can use up oxygen in the water, which can lead to fish kills.
draft.remember: Dams, weirs and irrigation reduce flows, causing salinity, algal blooms, fish kills and drying wetlands.

a.q: A river in the basin is warm, slow and low in summer, and farm fertiliser washes in. What is most likely to follow?
opts: An algal bloom
A cold, fast flow that keeps algae away
A flood that mixes the water quickly
Water that stays cool and shaded
a.why: Warm, slow, low water with extra nutrients meets every condition for a bloom. The other options describe cold, fast or mixing water, which does not suit algae.
a.clue: Match the conditions in the question to what a bloom needs.

b.q: Irrigators take much more water from a basin river, so flows stay low for years. What is the most likely effect on salt?
opts: Salt is not flushed out and builds up in the river
Salt is washed out to sea faster
Salt levels fall as the river gets shallower
Salt is not affected by the amount of flow
b.why: Low flows no longer flush salt out to sea, and irrigation water can raise saline water tables. Both lead to more salt in the river and soil.
b.clue: Think about what a strong flow does to salt.

b.best: Salt is not flushed out and builds up in the river

a.q: Which conditions in a basin river make an algal bloom most likely?
opts: Warm, slow, low water with fertiliser washing in
Cool, fast, high water with fertiliser washing in
Warm, slow, low water with no extra nutrients
Cool, fast, high water with no extra nutrients
a.why: A bloom is most likely when the water is warm, slow and low and also has extra nutrients, such as fertiliser. Warm, slow, low water with no extra nutrients is tempting, but it is missing the nutrients that feed the algae.
a.clue: A bloom needs the right water and something to feed on.

b.q: Irrigators take much more water from a basin river, so flows stay low for years. What is the most likely effect on salt?
opts: Salt is no longer flushed out and builds up
Salt is flushed out to sea faster than before
Salt levels fall as the river gets shallower
Salt levels stay the same whatever the flow
b.why: Low flows no longer flush salt out to sea, and irrigation can raise saline water tables. Both lead to more salt in the river and soil. A shallower river does not mean less salt, because the salt is not being carried away.
b.clue: Think about what a strong flow does to salt.
